readerTitle: Two owners, two orders, 400 mugs: who gets the final say?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방용품 소매점, 일정 관리 앱) · 모든 수치와 인물은 설명용
insight: 공동창업자 사이의 역할은 '누가 무슨 일을 하는가'보다 '어떤 결정을 누가 최종적으로 내리는가'로 나눠야 한다.
misconception: 지분이 같고 서로 믿는 사이라면 모든 결정을 함께 내리는 것이 가장 공정하고 안전하다.

sources.text: 조직 운영의 일반 원칙 (결정 유형별 단일 결정권자, 의견 제공자와 결정권자 구분)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 인물, 수치(머그컵 200개씩 두 번 주문, 총 400개)는 가상입니다. 실제 연구나 기업 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다.
특정 상표 프레임워크(예: RAPID, RACI)의 이름은 가이드 원칙에 따라 쓰지 않고 원리만 설명했습니다. 편집 과정에서 이름이 추가되지 않도록 확인하세요.
공동창업자 간 계약이나 주주간 계약의 법적 효력은 국가마다 다르므로 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않게 '서면으로 적어 둔다' 수준으로만 표현했습니다.

cards.title: Two owners, two orders, 400 mugs
body: Maya and Tom co-own a small kitchenware shop. On Monday, two trucks arrive. Each brings 200 of the same blue mugs.
Maya ordered them on Thursday. Tom ordered them on Friday. Both were trying to help. Now the stockroom is full and the cash is gone.

image.label: Two delivery trucks unloading identical boxes at a small shop
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트 스타일. 작은 주방용품 가게 앞에 배송 트럭 두 대가 나란히 서서 똑같은 파란 머그컵 상자를 내리고 있음. 가게 문 앞에서 두 공동창업자가 서로를 놀란 얼굴로 쳐다봄. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How should Maya and Tom stop this happening again?
body: They own the shop 50/50 and trust each other. Both like talking to suppliers. Which fix would you pick?

options.text: Agree to check with each other before every order
options.feedback: It prevents double orders, but every reorder now waits for two busy people. Small decisions slow down, and one missed text still causes trouble.

options.text: Make one of them the final decider on stock, and the other gives input
options.feedback: Orders stay fast and no one is shut out. The cost is that one partner has to accept losing the final say on something they enjoy.

options.text: Take turns: Maya orders in odd weeks, Tom in even weeks
options.feedback: It looks fair, but each person can undo the other's plan next week. Nobody owns the result, so nobody learns from it.

cards.title: They split the work, not the decisions.
body: Maya and Tom had talked about roles. Maya ran the shop floor. Tom did the books. Both did "buying".
But a role like "buying" hides many decisions: what to stock, how much, from whom, at what price. They never said who makes the **final call** on each one.
So both made it. Neither was wrong to act. The gap was in the agreement, not the people.

cards.title: Decision rights
body: **Decision rights** say who makes the final call on each kind of decision. Others can advise, push back or be told afterwards. But one person decides.
Tasks can be shared. Final calls work best with one owner each. For a few big decisions, the owners decide together, on purpose.

image.label: Simple table matching decision types to one decider
image.brief: 깔끔한 표 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 열에 "Stock and suppliers", "Shop layout", "Prices", "Taking a loan". 오른쪽 열에 각 결정의 담당자 "Tom", "Maya", "Maya", "Both". 'Both' 칸만 다른 색으로 강조.

cards.title: Four questions for every important decision.
body: Maya and Tom sit down with a coffee and a sheet of paper. For each recurring decision, they answer:
list: **Who must be asked first?** Their view is heard, but it isn't a veto
**Who just needs to know?** Told after, not before
**What goes to both of us?** Rare, big, hard-to-undo calls, like debt or a second shop
cards.callout: Tom takes stock. Maya takes prices. Mugs now arrive once.
cards.softwareNote: In a software startup, the same list might cover what to build next, which customers to sign, hiring and spending limits. Writing it down early matters more as the team grows.

cards.title: Equal partners don't need equal say on everything.
body: Many co-founders avoid this conversation. Giving one person the final call feels like ranking them.
It's the reverse. Clear decision rights let each partner move quickly in their area without asking permission. Respect shows up in the consulting step, not in a shared veto.
Without clear rights, the loudest or most available partner ends up deciding by default. That is less fair, not more.

cards.title: A decider still has to listen.
body: Decision rights fail if the owner stops consulting. A partner who is never asked will stop offering ideas, then start resenting the arrangement.
They also go stale. The split that fits a two-person shop may not fit a team of twelve. Review it when something big changes, such as a new hire or a new location.
And they don't end disagreements. They only make clear how a disagreement gets settled.

cards.title: Now it's a scheduling app.
body: Priya leads product. Sam leads sales. They agreed that Priya owns what gets built. A large clinic chain will sign if the app adds a custom report. Sam wants it now. Priya thinks it pulls the team off its plan. What should happen?

options.text: Whoever feels more strongly wins this one
options.feedback: It settles today's argument but teaches both founders that pressure beats agreements. The next dispute gets louder.

options.text: Priya decides, after hearing Sam's full case on revenue and timing
options.feedback: The agreed owner decides and the sales view gets a real hearing. Sam may lose this one, but he knows how the call was made.

options.text: Ask the clinic chain how important the report really is, then decide
options.feedback: Useful input for Priya's decision. But the customer can't own your product plan, and the founders still need to know who decides.

cards.softwareNote: Deals that need product changes are a classic gray zone between sales and product. Naming an owner for them in advance saves many late-night arguments.

cards.title: Name one decider for every important call.
body: Shared work is fine. Shared final calls cause double orders, slow choices and quiet resentment. Decide who decides, who gets asked, and what stays joint.
**Try it today:** list five decisions your business makes every month. Write one name next to each. Any decision with two names, or none, is your next conversation.
